turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on back, I'll grab vitals real quick. You look pretty wiped.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I've been out there forever and I itch, so yeah, let's just do this.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. Blood pressure is one twenty eight over seventy six, pulse 88, temp ninety eight point four fahrenheit, oxygen ninety eight percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Fine.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr. Shah. Sorry, the 10 was a parking lot. What brings you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): This rash. It itches like crazy between my fingers and right where my pants sit at my waist.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse at night. I am not sleeping and I'm snapping at everybody.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Umm. How long's that been going on?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Err. Two weeks? I can't tell you the day it started.
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Longer. More like a month, at least. She's been scratching since before the holiday weekend, I've been at the house helping.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay so somewhere between a couple weeks and a month. Who else at home is itching?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband. And my little boy, he's six, he keeps scratching his wrists.
[SEG0013] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The boy was up half the night. I heard him.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Is the rash oozing or crusting?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Oozing, umm, sometimes, not really.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any trouble breathing? Chest pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines do you take?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the Metformine for my sugar. Five hundred milligrams, morning and night.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, diabetes, we'll leave that. Have you been putting anything on the rash?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0024] person_4 (CAREGIVER): There was a tube of hydrocortazone from the drugstore. She used it maybe three nights.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah and I stopped. Didn't do a thing, so don't put down that I'm on it.
[SEG0026] person_4 (CAREGIVER): My sister had the same crawlies last winter, her and her little girl, different house. I was over there every night after work.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Can we not. I'm tired and I don't care about your sister.
[SEG0028] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry. The 405 was brutal though, hour and ten minutes from Inglewood.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): I sat on the 10 by the interchange, a lane was closed. Everybody was honking.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And it's already hot. My AC is dying. Had the Dodgers on, they blew the ninth again.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't care about baseball.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ha, alright, fair. Let me look at your hands and your waist.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yeah. Little burrows between the fingers, and the waist is scratched raw. I don't see spreading redness like a skin infection.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Feels like something's crawling. Is it in my blood?

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not in your blood. What I'm thinking is scabies. The tiny mites burrow into the top layer of skin, and the itch is your immune system reacting to them, firing at the mite proteins. It roars up at night when you're warm in bed.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Mites. So my kid has them too. Wonderful.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Very likely. Everyone in the house gets treated the same night, otherwise you pass it back and forth.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): The cream is permetrin, five percent. You coat from the neck down, every inch, between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the soles of the feet.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): All of that? I'm already exhausted.

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Put it on at bedtime, leave it eight to fourteen hours, wash it off in the morning. Then you do the exact same thing again in one week, because one round can miss the eggs.
[SEG0041] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I don't live there, I'm only days. Do I have to use it?

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not you, unless you had long skin-to-skin contact. The parents treat the boy the same night, same cream. Bag stuffed animals and coats you can't wash for three days. Sheets, towels, clothes from the last three days, hot wash and a hot dryer.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not rewashing the whole closet.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): You don't have to. Just what touched skin. And the itch can hang on two or three weeks after the mites are dead, that's the skin still reacting, not you failing the treatment.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): If I'm still clawing in two weeks I will be furious.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled after that second treatment, I might do a skin scraping to confirm. I'm not ordering one today.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll have them book you back in two weeks either way, so we're not guessing from the hallway.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Can I get the cream today?
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. We'll send the permetrin to the pharmacy, a tube for you, and I'll note tubes for your husband and your son. And stop the hydrocortazone, no more of that.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): I can send it. Which pharmacy?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): CVS on Western. I'm not standing in a long line, just so you know.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): I'll flag it. And nobody's changing the Metformine, that stays.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. If you get swelling or you can't breathe after the cream, stop it and get seen, that would be a reaction. Otherwise I will see you in two weeks.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Just get me the cream. I need to sleep.

spec.situation: Itchy rash between fingers and at the waist, worse at night, partner and child also itch; permethrin cream explained step by step; household treatment and washing advice.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Permethrin 5% planned and repeated in one week; 'once at bedtime' omits overnight 8-14 hours and second application.

bad.reason: Doctor notes no spreading redness, but not specifically limited to the waist.
